personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Dumbledore is defined by a distinctive voice: warmly witty, gently oblique, occasionally mischievous, but capable of steely firmness and cold disappointment. He speaks with erudition and unusual precision — capable of long, architecturally constructed arguments — but also of sudden deflating humor ('I enjoy Acid Pops'). He is characteristically calm under threat, uses pleasantries as instruments of social control (his visit to the Dursleys, his conversation with Voldemort), and deploys charm with visible awareness of its own artificiality. His firmness with Snape on the Astronomy Tower, his cold disappointment when Harry fails to retrieve the Slughorn memory, and his brisk redirections of Harry's questions all show a man who does not always explain himself but who chooses his moments. He also shows genuine emotion: the near-watery eyes when Harry declares himself 'Dumbledore's man through and through,' and the grief in 'I wish I could, Tom… I wish I could' are not concealed. His flaws are present too — his tendency to withhold information, his arguably arrogant confidence in his own judgment, his admission that his mistakes 'tend to be correspondingly huger.' He is not warm in a simple way; he is complex, self-aware, and calculating even when being kind.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film Dumbledore (Michael Gambon, carrying forward from GoF) preserves many of these surface traits with reasonable faithfulness in HBP. The wry humor is present: 'Being me has its privileges,' 'I once knew a Muggle girl from Liverpool with hair like spun silk,' the lingering over the knitting patterns magazine, his droll aside that Harry might be 'the Chosen One' while introducing him to Slughorn. The calm authority is intact — his manner with Draco on the tower ('I often talk aloud to myself… that which sounds sane at a whisper can seem utterly mad when said for all the world to hear'), his measured response to being Disarmed, his pleasantry toward Bellatrix. The firmness with Snape on the Astronomy Tower scene is present and well-executed. The visit to the orphanage shows his characteristic mix of gentleness, shrewd observation, and moral seriousness toward young Riddle. The film's Dumbledore is recognizably witty, controlled, perceptive, and kind.
personality_voice.difference: Several meaningful voice traits are either absent or diminished in the film. The book's Dumbledore delivers lengthy, philosophically layered speeches — notably the extended lecture on the prophecy, love, and choice (book scenes 987–999) and the multi-session pedagogical framework of the Pensieve lessons with their careful didacticism — which the film compresses significantly. His cold disappointment when Harry fails to retrieve the Slughorn memory is present in the film but considerably briefer, losing the sustained silence that felt 'worse than anything' and the precision of his rebuke. The moment of near-visible emotion when Harry says he is 'Dumbledore's man through and through' is entirely absent in the film corpus (the Scrimgeour Christmas conversation is not in the film). His self-deprecating acknowledgment of his own errors ('my mistakes tend to be correspondingly huger,' the admission of being 'woefully wrong as Humphrey Belcher') are absent. His explicit verbal articulation of his philosophy of love and free will — a cornerstone of his characterization in the books — is stripped to almost nothing. The film also lacks his occasional irritability (his impatient 'Yes, Harry, blessed as I am with extraordinary brainpower…' and the moment he sounds 'impatient' with Harry over Snape). The film Dumbledore is somewhat more uniformly warm and less multi-textured.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — wit, calm, authority, moral seriousness, strategic obliqueness — is well-preserved. The loss of his philosophical voice and the flattening of his occasional irritability and self-aware arrogance constitute a secondary-trait simplification rather than a fundamental alteration. The score sits at the high end of the 18–22 band.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In HBP, Dumbledore's narrative function is multifold and highly active: (1) He is the primary architect of the Horcrux investigation — identifying, collecting, and interpreting memories, theorizing Voldemort's soul-splitting strategy, and physically retrieving the ring Horcrux. (2) He is Harry's pedagogical mentor in the most intensive and consequential sense — the Pensieve lessons do not merely inform Harry but constitute the strategic framework for the entire final arc. (3) He is the only person who knows the full shape of what must be done, and who wills Harry into the position of understanding it. (4) He engineers Slughorn's return and tasks Harry with extracting the memory, deploying Harry as his instrument. (5) He directly confronts Malfoy on the tower and makes the active choice to engage him, protect Harry (by immobilizing him), and attempt to turn Malfoy. (6) His death is itself an agency-rich act — the choice to drink the potion, the pre-arranged condition of obedience, the wordless Petrificus on Harry. These are not passive events; he is the story's prime mover in HBP.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Dumbledore's core agency across most of these functions. The Horcrux investigation architecture is intact: he collects memories, explains their significance, deploys Harry to extract Slughorn's, and leads Harry to the cave. The cave sequence itself preserves his agency — he finds the entrance, unlocks the blood barrier himself, detects the hidden boat, directs Harry throughout, and (in the theatrical cut) he is the one who summons fire to repel the Inferi. His choice to immobilize Harry on the tower and engage Malfoy alone is preserved. His death remains a consequential, willed act.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several specific acts of agency are reduced or modified. The sustained, multi-session pedagogical architecture of the book's Pensieve lessons — five or more extended sessions, each carefully building the theory — is compressed into what feels like two or three encounters in the film, and Dumbledore's explicit discursive control of Harry's education is substantially reduced. Notably, the scene in which Dumbledore coldly impresses upon Harry the gravity of failing to retrieve the Slughorn memory is present but abbreviated, losing some of the pedagogical authority. The scene in which Dumbledore explains in extended detail his theory of the Horcruxes — the locket, the cup, Nagini, the possible Ravenclaw/Gryffindor object, the full intellectual architecture — is heavily compressed in the film (the ring/diary scene in the film is a compressed stand-in). The film also removes the scene where Dumbledore explicitly tells Harry he has 'earned the right' to accompany him, which in the book is an active confirmation of Harry's agency development. Also absent is Dumbledore's active intervention in Scrimgeour's attempts to use Harry — the book's Dumbledore is fighting on multiple political fronts simultaneously, a dimension of his agency the film reduces to near-nothing. His function as protector of Harry from the Ministry is noted in dialogue but not dramatized. These are genuine reductions in the breadth of his agency, though his central functions survive.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The core agency is preserved but noticeably compressed. The five or six Pensieve session arc is condensed, some transferred pedagogical weight goes to on-screen text compression. No single act of agency is transferred to another character (Harry still retrieves the memory, Dumbledore still leads the cave mission). This is a compression-based penalty, not a transfer-based one. Score sits in the 14–17 band.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dumbledore's motivations in HBP are legible and layered. He is driven by: (1) a long-term strategic purpose — the need to understand Voldemort's Horcruxes well enough to destroy them and enable Harry to defeat him — which he pursues with quiet obsession over years of dangerous solo investigation; (2) a pedagogical duty toward Harry specifically, which includes deliberate choices about what to reveal and when; (3) a complex mix of trust and control in his relationship with Snape — he trusts Snape completely, but the book hints at the weight of that trust and the argument we hear about; (4) a self-awareness about his own fallibility ('I make mistakes like the next man… my mistakes tend to be correspondingly huger'); (5) a philosophical commitment to love, free will, and human choice as the ultimate weapons against Voldemort — not merely an opinion but the motivating thesis of his entire approach to Harry's education. The cave mission is motivated not just by the Horcrux but by his desire to bring Harry actively into the fight, to give him 'the right.' His internal conflict around Snape — trusting him completely while also being visibly, irritably firm with him — is understated but present.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the main motivational outline. Dumbledore is clearly driven by the Horcrux hunt, by his investment in Harry's development, and by the strategic necessity of Slughorn's true memory. His trust of Snape is stated ('I will not negotiate this with you, Severus… you agreed') and dramatically consequential at the tower. His self-awareness about the danger to Harry is present in the tower scene and the cave conditions.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The philosophical dimension of his motivation — his belief in love as power, his explicit argument that the prophecy does not compel Harry but that Harry chooses — is entirely absent from the film. This is not a minor stylistic omission; in the books it is the culminating expression of why Dumbledore has conducted these lessons the way he has. The Scrimgeour conversation (in which Harry's loyalty to Dumbledore is actively dramatized) is absent, which removes a dimension of Dumbledore's political motivation. The self-deprecating acknowledgment of fallibility is absent, weakening the internal tension between his extraordinary confidence and his genuine humility. His motivation in giving Harry 'the right' to join him — actively framed as a reward and a pedagogical milestone in the books — is present in the film but reduced to a straightforward promise kept. The film's Dumbledore is motivationally coherent but philosophically thinner.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but still correct in their essential shape. The strategic and relational motivations survive; the philosophical dimension is lost. This is an 11–13 penalty — simplified but not wrong.

character_arc.book_baseline: Dumbledore's arc in HBP is unusual: it is largely a revelation arc rather than a change arc. He begins already knowing vast amounts, and the books progressively disclose his knowledge to Harry and the reader. His visible arc within the book is: (1) the gradual physical deterioration from the ring Horcrux injury, culminating in the cave; (2) the slow transfer of strategic knowledge and responsibility to Harry through the Pensieve sessions — a deliberate pedagogical project with a clear endpoint; (3) the final act of self-sacrifice on the tower, understood (by the reader, eventually) as chosen rather than merely suffered. His arc also includes the explicit articulation of his philosophy of love and choice in the final lesson, which is both its climax and its farewell. His death does not reverse his arc but completes it: he has done what he set out to do in this book.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves the physical deterioration arc (the blackened hand is present throughout, commented on), the pedagogical transfer of knowledge via Pensieve, the cave mission as both the physical and narrative climax of his HBP arc, and his death as a consequential endpoint. The final lesson — the Horcrux revelation session — is retained in compressed form. His death on the tower is staged faithfully.
character_arc.difference: The completion of the pedagogical arc — the final lesson in which Dumbledore explicitly articulates his philosophy and the full meaning of the prophecy ('you are setting too much store by the prophecy') — is absent from the film. This means the arc's intended endpoint, the moment at which Dumbledore has finished what he set out to do with Harry's education, is truncated. The transfer of understanding — not just strategic information but philosophical orientation — is incomplete in the film. The arc is compressed but its essential shape survives; what is missing is its thematic resolution. The film does include a partial analog in the Horcrux discussion scene but without the extended love/prophecy debate that gives the arc its full meaning.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is present and recognizable, but the thematic culmination is missing. This is a compression that changes the meaning of the endpoint somewhat — Dumbledore's arc in the film ends at physical death without the philosophical handoff being fully completed. Score is in the 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Three relationships are primary in HBP. (1) Dumbledore–Harry: deeply asymmetric in knowledge but genuinely mutual in respect and trust; the most important relationship in the book, structured as mentorship with explicit warmth, occasional paternal tenderness (the broom shed scene about Sirius, the emotional weight of 'I am very touched, Harry'), and real pedagogical purpose. Dumbledore's investment in Harry is not just instrumental — he is genuinely proud of him, visibly moved by his loyalty, and chooses him as the person who can succeed where Dumbledore himself cannot. (2) Dumbledore–Snape: highly complex — absolute trust on Dumbledore's part, expressed through a firmness that borders on coercion ('you agreed'), and Snape's visible resentment under the obligation; the overheard argument ('he didn't want to do it anymore') and Hagrid's account of the row add tension. Dumbledore's trust is a conscious, active choice, not naivety — he knows what he is asking. (3) Dumbledore–Voldemort (Tom Riddle): mediated through memory, but their direct encounter in Dumbledore's own memory (the Hog's Head meeting) shows a relationship of mutual respect-as-antagonism — Dumbledore calling him 'Tom,' refusing his framing, the sadness of 'I wish I could, Tom.' This relationship illuminates Dumbledore's most important quality: his refusal to abandon the person beneath the monster, even while being clear about the monster.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Dumbledore–Harry relationship is well-preserved in the film's theatrical cut: the mentorship warmth, the trust, the quiet pride, the practical conditions of obedience. The film's Astronomy Tower scene ('At times I still see the small boy from the cupboard') adds a tender dimension not literally in the books but consistent with the dynamic. The Dumbledore–Snape relationship is preserved via the overheard Astronomy Tower argument, which captures the tension of an obligation Snape resents and Dumbledore enforces. The Dumbledore–Voldemort relationship via memory is present (the orphanage memory is faithfully rendered).
key_relationships.difference: The Dumbledore–Harry relationship loses two significant emotional beats from the book: the Sirius conversation in the broom shed (a moment of genuine emotional intimacy, Dumbledore consoling Harry about the loss of his godfather — the most openly warm exchange in their HBP relationship) is absent from the film; and the 'Dumbledore's man through and through' conversation (and Dumbledore's near-tears response, 'I am very touched') is absent, the Scrimgeour Christmas scene not being in the film. These are not incidental — they are the primary evidence in HBP that the relationship has genuine emotional warmth beyond pedagogy. Their absence flattens the dynamic somewhat toward functional mentor/student. The Dumbledore–Snape relationship is handled adequately but the multi-layered book dynamic (the row, the earlier overheard exchange reported by Hagrid, the implication that Dumbledore argued with Snape and Snape felt 'overworked') is reduced to a single confrontation. The Dumbledore–Voldemort memory relationship is preserved in the orphanage scene but the second major memory encounter (Dumbledore's own memory of Voldemort's return visit to Hogwarts — the Hog's Head conversation) is absent from the film, removing one of the richest illustrations of how Dumbledore handles Voldemort.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Two key emotional beats in the primary relationship are missing (broom shed / Sirius; 'Dumbledore's man' moment). The Voldemort-return-to-Hogwarts memory is absent. These are genuine alterations to the emotional texture of the relationships, bringing the score into the 5–6 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The book Dumbledore is rich in complexity that resists summary. He is simultaneously: a man of extraordinary wisdom who withholds information for reasons that are partly protective and partly controlling; a mentor who admits his own errors but rarely changes course as a result; a moral philosopher whose views on love and choice are stated with absolute conviction but tested nowhere more severely than in his trust of Snape; a man capable of cold disappointment and sustained silence as discipline (the Slughorn memory rebuke); a figure with genuine political savvy who maneuvers against Scrimgeour while publicly appearing disengaged; a person who finds the Dursleys genuinely funny and uses social manipulation with visible enjoyment; and ultimately, a man who has chosen his death with some foreknowledge and structured the entire year's pedagogy as a farewell gift. His famous intellectual humility ('I may be as woefully wrong as Humphrey Belcher') coexists with his obvious confidence in his own judgment. His refusal to tell Harry about the injury for much of the book, his enigmatic 'Horcrux hunt' absences, his deliberate management of information across the Pensieve sessions — all these build a portrait of a deeply strategic, unsentimental intelligence beneath the warm exterior.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves a good deal of this. The strategic obliqueness is intact (his refusal to explain the injury, 'the tale is thrilling but now is not the time,' 'I would rather not divulge any more just yet'; his letting Slughorn come to him rather than pressing). The Dursley social manipulation is preserved in the film versions of that encounter (though the film's Dursley visit is cut from HBP specifically — the theatrical HBP does not include the Dursley scene). The cave sequence preserves his decisive, systematic approach to magical detection ('magic always leaves traces') and his self-sacrifice logic ('I am much older, much cleverer, and much less valuable'). The tower sequence preserves his composure under existential threat and his choice to engage Malfoy rather than simply wait.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film loses: (1) The extended philosophical argument about love and the prophecy — the most sophisticated articulation of what makes Dumbledore Dumbledore in these books. (2) The Scrimgeour political maneuvering — his active resistance to Ministry co-option, demonstrated through Harry's reported conversations, is entirely absent. (3) The sustained pedagogical architecture of five-plus Pensieve sessions, with their cumulative building of both knowledge and Dumbledore's analytical method. (4) The Slughorn memory rebuke scene — while present in the film, it is brief, and the sustained silence that characterizes Dumbledore's disappointment in the book is truncated. (5) The broom shed Sirius conversation, showing Dumbledore's capacity for genuine emotional intimacy and his understanding of Harry's grief. (6) The Voldemort-return-to-Hogwarts memory, which is one of the richest scenes in the corpus for showing how Dumbledore reads and handles Voldemort — his refusal to use the name, his ironic pleasantries, his directness ('Let us speak openly'), and his final sadness. (7) The explicit articulation of his own fallibility and its coexistence with his confidence. (8) The Dursley scene (the HBP book scene at Privet Drive), which shows Dumbledore at his most playful and socially manipulative. These are not merely decorative losses; they collectively account for the majority of what makes book-Dumbledore philosophically and emotionally distinctive from a merely competent film mentor figure.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The losses are substantial and cumulative: the philosophical dimension, the political dimension, the emotional intimacy dimension, and one of the two major memory encounters are all gone or severely reduced. The remaining material is faithful as far as it goes, but it does not go far enough to constitute a substantially complete portrait. Score is 10 — noticeable simplification with important nuances and the most philosophically rich material missing.

lost_or_transferred_material: Extended Pensieve pedagogy across five-plus sessions — the cumulative intellectual architecture of Dumbledore's Horcrux theory is compressed to approximately two encounters in the film

The prophecy/love/free will lecture (book scenes 987–999) — the thematic culmination of Dumbledore's pedagogical arc, explicitly arguing that love is the decisive power and that the prophecy does not compel Harry, is entirely absent from the film

The 'Dumbledore's man through and through' Christmas conversation with Scrimgeour — Dumbledore's near-tears response ('I am very touched, Harry') is absent; this scene also contains his political maneuvering against the Ministry
The broom shed conversation about Sirius — Dumbledore's most emotionally intimate exchange with Harry in HBP, acknowledging the brutality of Sirius's death and Harry's grief, is absent from the film
Dumbledore's extended visit to the Dursleys (Privet Drive chapter) — showing his social manipulation, wit, firmness with the Dursleys, and playful side, is not part of the HBP film

Dumbledore's own memory of Voldemort's return-to-Hogwarts visit (the Hog's Head scene) — one of the corpus's richest illustrations of their adversarial dynamic, Dumbledore's refusal to use the name 'Voldemort,' his ironic pleasantries, his direct challenge ('Let us speak openly'), and his final sadness, is absent from the film
The Slughorn memory rebuke — present in the film but substantially shortened, losing the sustained silence, the cold disappointment as instrument of discipline, and Harry's shame response

Dumbledore's argument with Snape reported by Hagrid and Harry's subsequent multi-layered interpretation — the political/trust complexity of that relationship is reduced to the single Astronomy Tower overheard exchange

Dumbledore's explicit self-deprecating acknowledgment of his own fallibility ('my mistakes tend to be correspondingly huger') — absent from the film, removing a key marker of his intellectual self-awareness

The full Gaunt family memory sequence (Ogden's visit, Bob Ogden's memory, Morfin's memory, the full Hepzibah Smith memory) — several Pensieve sessions are not present in the HBP film, substantially reducing the Horcrux theory's evidential base as Dumbledore constructs it
The condition under which Dumbledore tells Harry he has 'earned the right' to join him — explicitly a pedagogical reward in the books — is absent from the film version (present only in a cut scene)
The line 'I am not worried, Harry. I am with you' — present only in a cut scene and therefore not in the theatrical film
score_caps_applied: Cap 2 (score above 80 if key relationships change substantially) — applied: the loss of the broom shed Sirius scene, the 'Dumbledore's man through and through' emotional beat, and the Voldemort-return memory constitutes substantial change to key relationships, preventing a score above 80

Cap 1 (score above 85 if films remove a major part of complexity, agency, contradiction, or narrative function) — applied: the loss of the philosophical dimension (prophecy/love lecture), the political dimension (Scrimgeour maneuvering), and the full Pensieve pedagogical arc removes major complexity, reinforcing the cap below 85
key_observations: The film's Dumbledore is a faithful and well-performed version of the character's surface — the wit, the calm authority, the strategic obliqueness, the warmth toward Harry, the composure under threat, and the decisive self-sacrifice are all present and recognizable. The cave sequence, the orphanage memory, the Astronomy Tower confrontation with Malfoy, and the firmness with Snape are all effective film moments that track closely to the books. However, the film loses the character's most philosophically distinctive dimension: the extended argument that love is the decisive power and that the prophecy does not compel but that Harry freely chooses — the thematic culmination of everything Dumbledore has done in HBP. It also loses two of his most emotionally intimate moments with Harry (the broom shed Sirius conversation, the 'Dumbledore's man' response) and one of the richest memory encounters (Voldemort's return to Hogwarts). The result is a Dumbledore who is recognizable and largely faithful in action and demeanor but philosophically thinner and emotionally less fully drawn than his book counterpart. He functions as a mentor and strategist; what the film cannot quite capture is that he is also a moral philosopher, a political operator, and a man capable of genuine, visible grief and tenderness. The total of 78 reflects a strong but incomplete adaptation — faithful where present, but with meaningful losses that reduce the character's full complexity.
